Draping Style.name: Panchakacham (5-Yard Traditional Drape)
Draping Style.description: A more elaborate five-part draping style where the dhoti is wrapped, tucked, and pleated to resemble loose trousers with a rear flap, traditionally worn by priests and during formal Tamil Brahmin rituals.
Draping Style.materials: Cotton or silk, single long panel (veshti)
Draping Style.notes: Requires practiced skill to drape correctly; largely worn today only by priests and at select rituals.

Draping Style.name: Kacha (Bengali Dhoti Drape)
Draping Style.description: A distinctive Bengali draping technique where the front pleats are pulled between the legs and tucked at the back waist, creating a loose, trouser-like fall unique to Bengali dhoti-wearing tradition.
Draping Style.notes: Closely associated with Bengali groom's wedding attire, paired with a punjabi (kurta) and often a red-bordered dhoti.

Draping Style.name: Simple Waist-Tie Drape
Draping Style.description: The most basic drape — wrapped once around the waist and tied or tucked without the multiple pleated folds of ceremonial styles — worn for comfort in everyday domestic settings.
Draping Style.notes: The most common way dhotis are worn casually at home across most regions of India.

Draping Style.name: Half-Dhoti (Angavastram Pair)
Draping Style.description: A shorter dhoti draped to fall around knee-to-mid-calf length, typically worn with a matching angavastram (shoulder cloth) rather than a full-length drape.
Draping Style.notes: A practical, breathable choice suited to South Indian climate for daily temple visits.

Fabric & Weave.name: Cotton Dhoti
Fabric & Weave.description: Woven from plain white or off-white cotton, the most common and breathable dhoti fabric suited to everyday wear across India's varied climates.
Fabric & Weave.notes: The default fabric for daily and semi-formal dhoti wear due to comfort and easy upkeep.

Fabric & Weave.name: Silk Dhoti (Pattu Veshti)
Fabric & Weave.description: Woven from silk, often with a zari border matching the regional saree tradition (such as Kanjeevaram-style borders), worn for weddings and major festive or religious occasions.
Fabric & Weave.notes: Often purchased as a matching pair with an angavastram carrying the same zari border.

Fabric & Weave.name: Mundu (Kerala White Dhoti)
Fabric & Weave.occasion: Onam, weddings, temple visits, daily wear
Fabric & Weave.description: Kerala's distinct dhoti variant, typically pristine white or cream cotton with a simple gold (kasavu) or coloured border, worn double-folded at the waist rather than pleated between the legs.
Fabric & Weave.notes: Considered a distinct garment name (mundu) though functionally part of the wider dhoti family.

Fabric & Weave.name: Silk-Cotton Blend Dhoti
Fabric & Weave.description: Combines silk and cotton yarns to offer some of the sheen and drape of silk at a lighter weight and lower cost than pure silk dhotis.
Fabric & Weave.notes: A popular mid-range choice for festive functions where a pure silk dhoti isn't necessary.

Border & Colour Tradition.name: Zari-Border Dhoti
Border & Colour Tradition.description: Carries a gold or silver zari border along the length, ranging from a slim decorative line to a wide, heavily worked border for bridegroom wear.
Border & Colour Tradition.notes: Border width is often used as an informal signal of formality — wider borders for weddings, narrower for temple visits.

Border & Colour Tradition.name: Colour-Bordered Dhoti (Kaavi/Red Border)
Border & Colour Tradition.description: Features a solid colour border — commonly red, maroon, or mustard — instead of metallic zari, offering a simpler but still festive alternative.
Border & Colour Tradition.notes: A more affordable and everyday alternative to zari-bordered dhotis, common for regular temple wear.

Border & Colour Tradition.name: Plain White Dhoti
Border & Colour Tradition.occasion: Daily wear, mourning rites, religious observance
Border & Colour Tradition.description: A borderless or minimally bordered plain white dhoti, worn for daily comfort as well as for religious rites and mourning ceremonies where unadorned white is considered appropriate.
Border & Colour Tradition.notes: The most versatile dhoti type, appropriate across the widest range of everyday and ritual contexts.

Regional Variants.name: Dhotar (Maharashtrian Dhoti)
Regional Variants.description: Draped in a distinct Maharashtrian style with pleats tucked to create a dhoti-cum-trouser shape, traditionally paired with a pheta (turban) for full ceremonial dress.
Regional Variants.notes: Often paired with a matching pheta and a Nehru-style jacket for weddings and cultural events.

Regional Variants.name: Dhuti (Assamese/Bengali Everyday Variant)
Regional Variants.description: A regional variant worn across eastern India, generally lighter and simpler in drape than the ceremonial Bengali kacha style, used for both daily and festive contexts.
Regional Variants.notes: Distinguished from the formal kacha drape by its simpler, quicker tie.

Regional Variants.name: Panche (Karnataka Dhoti)
Regional Variants.occasion: Daily wear, temple visits, festive functions
Regional Variants.description: Karnataka's regional term and style for the dhoti, typically draped in a simple waist-tie style and often checked rather than plain, especially for daily wear.
Regional Variants.notes: Checked cotton panches are common daily wear, while plain white or zari-bordered versions are reserved for formal occasions.
